title.value: Conventional Biopsy and Sampling Techniques | source_page: 1 | source_excerpt: "Conventional Biopsy and Sampling Techniques"

diagnostic_approaches.name: Forceps biopsy (central endobronchial lesions)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Sampling cytohistological material from bronchoscopically visible airway lesions.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Open the forceps above the lesion, advance and push toward target, close firmly, then withdraw through the working channel; keep forceps close to bronchoscope tip.
limitations: Difficult to sample submucosal/peribronchial lesions or necrotic lesions
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Endobronchial lesions within visual range of the flexible bronchoscope.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: In central airway lesions, forceps biopsy yields sensitivity that is around 88%, based on a systematic review of 35 studies

diagnostic_approaches.name: Electrocautery biopsy forceps (hot forceps)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Proposed for sampling endobronchial lesions with the aim to prevent bleeding.
limitations: No evidence of reducing clinically relevant bleeding
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: there is no evidence that they may reduce the incidence of clinically relevant bleeding episodes, and their routine use is not warranted.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Cryobiopsy (central bronchogenic lesions)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Endobronchial biopsy of central bronchogenic lesions.
limitations: not enough evidence to recommend routine use.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Could be reserved for difficult cases when a first bronchoscopy has not been diagnostic.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: A definitive diagnosis was achieved in 85.1% with conventional forceps biopsy and in 95% of patients who underwent cryobiopsy ( p < 0.001)

diagnostic_approaches.name: Brushing (central endobronchial lesions)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Collect cytological material from bronchoscopically visible airway lesions.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Directly smear the brush onto a glass slide or place in saline and remove cells by vigorous shaking.
limitations: not indicated for submucosal or intraparietal lesions.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Used for bronchoscopically visible lesions; may be combined with biopsy.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: The average diagnostic yield from brushing is lower compared to forceps biopsy, with a sensitivity of 59% [37].

diagnostic_approaches.name: Bronchial washing (central airway lesions)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Sampling cells from central airway lesions.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Instill saline through the working channel and retrieve by suction.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: May be collected during bronchoscopy; examine if other specimens are not diagnostic.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: The sensitivity of washing for central lung cancer is lower than that obtained by biopsy or brushing, with an average value of 48% [37].

diagnostic_approaches.name: Brushing and washing for mycobacterial diseases
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Diagnosis of mycobacterial diseases.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Agitate brush in a sterile medium; collect washing in a sterile specimen trap.
limitations: Specimens are contaminated by oropharyngeal flora during transnasal/transoral passage.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: In suspected infectious conditions.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: The sensitivity of brushing and washing for the diagnosis of mycobacterial diseases is very high, and it has been reported to range from 58% to 96% [22].

diagnostic_approaches.name: Transbronchial needle aspiration (TBNA) for central bronchial lesions
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Sample deep mucosal and peribronchial components of central bronchial lesions.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Penetrate deep layers of mucosa/peribronchial area with the needle and aspirate target lesion.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Visible central lesions, especially infiltrative, hypervascular, or necrotic lesions.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: The sensitivity of TBNA for central bronchial lesions is reported to range from 68% to 91%, with values similar to those obtained by forceps biopsy [30].

diagnostic_approaches.name: Imprint cytology or biopsy rinse cytology (adjuncts to forceps biopsy)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Alternative processing of forceps biopsy samples.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Smear the biopsy on a slide (imprint cytology) or examine the biopsy rinse fluid cytologically.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: these techniques have not been validated and their use is not recommended.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Conventional forceps biopsy for central airway lesions
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Diagnosis of endobronchial pathology visible by bronchoscopy
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: High diagnostic yield; better sensitivity than other techniques when mucosal involvement is suggested.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: When the lesion pattern suggests mucosal involvement.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Biopsy forceps provide better sensitivity compared to other sampling techniques when the pattern of the lesion suggests mucosal involvement.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Transbronchial needle aspiration (TBNA) for central airway lesions
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Sampling submucosal/peribronchial disease; assess bleeding risk; sample necrotic lesions; predict surgical resection line; use after negative biopsy.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Allows assessment of tumoral spread around the main lesion.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Submucosal or peribronchial involvement; very vascularized tissue to test bleeding risk; large necrotic component; repeated bronchoscopy after first negative biopsy.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: TBNA may allow to predict the line of surgical resection, establishing the degree of tumoral spread around the main lesion [4].

diagnostic_approaches.name: Fluoroscopy-guided transbronchial approach to peripheral pulmonary lesions
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Guided sampling of peripheral nodules, masses, or infiltrates outside the bronchoscope’s visible range.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Use a rotating C-arm or biplane fluoroscope; assess AP and lateral views; wedge into segmental bronchus and advance instrument under fluoroscopic control.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Biplane control helps avoid misplacement anterior or posterior to the target.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Localized peripheral pulmonary pathology requiring precise instrument-to-lesion positioning.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: The sensitivity of the transbronchial approach to peripheral pulmonary lesions under ﬂuoroscopic guidance varies greatly... from 22% to 83%, with an overall value of 78% [36].

diagnostic_approaches.name: Lesion size effect on sensitivity (fluoroscopy-guided bronchoscopic approach)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Estimate expected sensitivity based on lesion size during fluoroscopy-guided bronchoscopic biopsy.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Smaller lesions have lower diagnostic yield than larger ones.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: When counseling yield expectations by lesion size before fluoroscopy-guided biopsy.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: A sensitivity ranging from 5% to 64% is reported for nodules less than 2 cm in diameter and from 30% to 75% for nodules greater than 2 cm,

diagnostic_approaches.name: TBNA for peripheral pulmonary lesions under fluoroscopic guidance
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Diagnostic sampling of peripheral pulmonary lesions, particularly for malignancy.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Use flexible TBNA needle through bronchoscope to penetrate lesions not involving mucosal surface.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Provides better sensitivity for malignancy than forceps biopsy or brushing; exclusive needle yield 8%–35%.
limitations: Cytology-only sampling may be less useful for benign disease diagnosis.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Peripheral lesions not involving mucosal surface or peribronchiolar location.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: the exclusive yield of the needle is reported to range from 8% to 35% [11].

diagnostic_approaches.name: Minimum number of transbronchial biopsy specimens (peripheral lesions)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Optimize diagnostic yield of peripheral bronchoscopy.
criteria_or_scoring: Obtain at least six biopsy specimens.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Take ≥6 biopsy samples during the procedure.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: More specimens improve yield.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: During transbronchial biopsy of peripheral lesions to maximize diagnostic yield.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: at least six biopsy specimens should be obtained for optimizing the results.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Combining sampling instruments for peripheral bronchoscopy
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Increase diagnostic yield compared to a single tool.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Use multiple instruments (e.g., needle plus forceps) in one procedure.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Combining instruments yields better results than a single tool.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Peripheral lesion sampling when feasible to improve yield.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: the association of more sampling instruments provides better results than those obtained with a single tool [12, 44].

diagnostic_approaches.name: Bronchial washing and bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) for localized peripheral lesions
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Cytologic diagnosis of localized peripheral lung lesions.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Very low sensitivity as stand-alone tests.
limitations: routine use not justified as add-on due to minimal incremental sensitivity.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: May be used without guidance systems; consider in infiltrative malignancy patterns.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: very low sensitivity in the case of localized peripheral lesions, with values ranging from 9% to 42% [36].

diagnostic_approaches.name: Incremental sensitivity of bronchial washing when added to brushing or biopsy
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Quantify additional diagnostic yield from adding washing to other instruments.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Increase in sensitivity by only 3%.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: As an adjunct to brushing or biopsy if performed.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: When performed together with brushing or biopsy, bronchial washing shows an increase insensitivity by only 3%.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Cryobiopsy for peripheral lung tumors
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Obtain larger, architecturally preserved tissue to improve diagnostic sensitivity and genotyping.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Use a 1.1 mm cryoprobe via transbronchial approach.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Better sensitivity and larger specimens than conventional forceps biopsy.
limitations: No studies comparing cryobiopsy vs. needle aspiration
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: When increased tissue volume/architecture is needed for diagnosis/genotyping.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: The better sensitivity and the greater specimens of cryobiopsy in comparison with conventional forceps biopsy have been demonstrated in several studies

diagnostic_approaches.name: CT bronchus sign
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Predict success of transbronchial biopsies based on lesion-airway relationship.
criteria_or_scoring: Image of bronchus leading to or contained within the lesion on thin-section CT.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Evaluate thin-section CT scan for a bronchus leading to or within the lesion.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Presence predicts higher success of transbronchial biopsies.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Before planning transbronchial biopsy of peripheral nodules.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: CT scan “bronchus sign,” that is the image of the bronchus leading to or contained within the lesion, visualized by thin-section CT scan, to predict the success of the transbronchial biopsies

diagnostic_approaches.name: Conventional transbronchial needle aspiration (cTBNA) for hilar–mediastinal lesions
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Sampling hilar–mediastinal lesions without endobronchial ultrasound; staging and diagnosis.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Choose puncture point from CT; insert perpendicularly using jabbing or pushing methods; aspirate; perform ≥4 aspirates per station.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Yield improves with number of aspirates up to four passes.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: When ultrasound technology is unavailable or not feasible.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: so that it is recommended to perform at least four aspirates at each lymph nodal station to optimize the yield.

diagnostic_approaches.name: cTBNA diagnostic yield for lung cancer staging
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Expected diagnostic sensitivity of cTBNA in mediastinal staging.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Post-1990s series generally exceed 70% sensitivity; mean about 78%.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Staging of lung cancer when performing cTBNA.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: papers published after the 1990s generally report values greater than 70%, with a mean value of 78% [4, 17, 20].

diagnostic_approaches.name: cTBNA sensitivity by lymph node size
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Estimate cTBNA yield based on lymph node size.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Yield increases with node size; limited for nodes <1 cm.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Pre-procedure counseling and planning for cTBNA.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: from a reported value of only 15% for targets less than 1 cm to about 80% for lesions of 2.0–2.5 cm.

diagnostic_approaches.name: EBUS-TBNA (endobronchial ultrasound-guided TBNA)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Real-time ultrasound-guided sampling of hilar–mediastinal lesions; mediastinal staging and diagnosis.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Linear ultrasound bronchoscope guidance with real-time needle sampling.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Advantages in sensitivity and ability to visualize small lymph nodes.
limitations: Ultrasound technology may be unavailable in some centers.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Mediastinal staging of lung cancer and diagnosis of lesions outside tracheobronchial tree.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: this technique has become the method of choice for the mediastinal staging of lung cancer and for diagnosis of lesions located outside the tracheobronchial tree [18].

diagnostic_approaches.name: TBNA specimen processing for molecular profiling (smear cytology plus cell-block)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Achieve complete molecular profile (including PD-L1) from TBNA samples.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Smear cytology plus cell-block; flush material in 10% neutral-buffered formalin.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Complete molecular profile achieved in 86.6% of 154 patients.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: When genotyping is needed from TBNA specimens.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: able to obtain a complete molecular proﬁle, including evaluation of PD-L1 expression, in 86.6% of 154 patients approached with transbronchial needle aspiration for peripheral cancer.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Other instruments for peripheral lesions (curette, suction catheter, needle brush, triple needle brush)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Alternative sampling methods for peripheral lesions.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: No evidence of utility compared to forceps or needle aspiration.
limitations: Lack of evidence for improved utility vs. standard tools.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: but there is no evidence in the literature of their real utility compared to biopsy forceps or needle aspiration.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Bronchial washing for central airway tumors
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Cytologic sampling in central airway tumors (adjunctive).
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Little value alone; may slightly improve sensitivity with other tools; routine use not recommended.
limitations: Low standalone utility in central tumors.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Adjunct to other sampling instruments if used.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Washing alone is of little value in the diagnosis of central airway tumors.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Conventional Transbronchial Needle Aspiration (TBNA)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Lung cancer staging; diagnosis of carcinomas with mediastinal involvement on CT without airway lesions; cytohistological qualification for mediastinal processes close to the airways.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Sample lymph nodes before the primary tumor; avoid puncturing mucosa involved by tumor; release suction before removing the needle; introduce/withdraw the needle with the tip completely retracted into the sheath.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Very high specificity; false positives very rarely reported; considered a very safe technique; complications rarely reported.
limitations: possible risk of puncturing large mediastinal vessels
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: For lung cancer staging and for mediastinal lesions seen on CT without airway lesions; for mediastinal diseases close to airways.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: The specificity of conventional TBNA is very high, ranging from 96% to 100%, and cases of false positive have been very rarely reported.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Conventional TBNA for sarcoidosis diagnosis
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Diagnosis of sarcoidosis; enhances bronchoscopy diagnostic yield, especially in stage I sarcoidosis.
criteria_or_scoring: Cytology: lymphocytes mixed with epithelioid cells and a multinucleated giant cell without necrosis.
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Needle inserted in the spur between the right upper lobe bronchus and the bronchus intermediate (case example).
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Improves diagnostic yield of bronchoscopy, particularly in stage I sarcoidosis.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Especially for stage I sarcoidosis.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: with a sensitivity greater than 70%, and this technique may improve the diagnostic yield of bronchoscopy by up to 90%, especially for stage I sarcoidosis

diagnostic_approaches.name: CT scan (mediastinal lymph node enlargement identification)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Shows lymph nodes enlargements to identify target stations.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Lymph nodes enlargements in subcarinal and bilateral hilar stations.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: CT scan shows lymph nodes enlargements in subcarinal and bilateral hilar stations.

treatment_algorithms.title: Management algorithm for bronchoscopic biopsy-induced bleeding
specific_recommendations: Rotate patient to lateral decubitus with bleeding side down.
Keep bronchoscope in place; apply continuous suction.
Instill ice-cold saline.
Instill epinephrine diluted 1:10,000 in 2–3 ml aliquots, up to three doses.
Use endobronchial tamponade with a balloon catheter (e.g., Fogarty).
Maintain a Fogarty balloon available in the bronchoscopy suite.
If bleeding source visible, consider low-energy laser or electrocautery with argon plasma.
If ineffective, consider intubation with rigid bronchoscope or large channel endotracheal tube.
If bleeding persists, consider selective intubation of the contralateral main bronchus.
As last resort, consider bronchial artery embolization or open surgical procedures.
decision_points_and_pathways: Bleeding occurs -> lateral decubitus (bleeding side down) + suction.
If ongoing -> ice-cold saline + epinephrine (1:10,000; 2–3 ml aliquots; max three doses).
If ongoing -> balloon tamponade (Fogarty).
If source visible -> low-energy laser/electrocautery with argon plasma.
If persistent -> intubate (rigid or large channel ET tube).
If persistent -> selective contralateral intubation.
If all fail -> bronchial artery embolization/open surgery.
treatment_algorithms.source_excerpt: epinephrine (diluted in a 1:10,000 mixture of normal saline and administered in 2–3 ml aliquots to a maximum of three doses)

treatment_algorithms.title: Fluoroscopy-guided transbronchial sampling of peripheral localized lesions
treatment_algorithms.condition: Peripheral localized pulmonary lesions (nodules/masses/infiltrates) outside visible bronchoscope range
specific_recommendations: Ensure guidance availability (rotating C-arm or biplane fluoroscope) for AP and lateral views.
Wedge the bronchoscope into the segmental bronchus leading to the lesion; steer under fluoroscopy.
Prefer TBNA for malignancy yield; combine with forceps to improve diagnosis of benign lesions.
Obtain ≥6 biopsy specimens to optimize sensitivity.
If multiple tools used, deploy the needle first, then forceps/brushing.
Evaluate CT 'bronchus sign' preprocedure to predict success.
For bleeding, maintain wedge position; use 4–7 Fr balloon catheter at the segmental orifice.
decision_points_and_pathways: CT suggests lesion beyond visible range -> Use fluoroscopic guidance (AP + lateral).
Needle vs forceps -> Prefer TBNA for malignancy; add forceps for suspected benign disease.
Need for higher yield -> Combine instruments and target ≥6 forceps samples.
If bleeding -> Wedge + balloon catheter; proceed to standard bleeding algorithm if persistent.
treatment_algorithms.patient_population_criteria: Adults with localized peripheral pulmonary lesions approached via bronchoscopy
treatment_algorithms.monitoring_requirements: Fluoroscopic AP and lateral control; hemodynamic and oxygenation monitoring
treatment_algorithms.source_excerpt: A rotating C-arm or a biplane fluoroscope must be available ... ≥6 biopsies ... needle first ... 'bronchus sign' ... balloon catheter (4–7 French).

clinical_guidelines.title: Avoid routine use of electrocautery biopsy forceps (hot forceps) for central endobronchial lesions
clinical_guidelines.condition: Central endobronchial lesions
specific_recommendations: Do not use hot forceps routinely for sampling central endobronchial lesions.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: there is no evidence that they may reduce the incidence of clinically relevant bleeding episodes, and their routine use is not warranted.

clinical_guidelines.title: Do not routinely use cryobiopsy for central bronchogenic lesions
clinical_guidelines.condition: Central bronchogenic lesions
specific_recommendations: Avoid routine use of cryobiopsy for central bronchogenic lesions.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: there is not enough evidence to recommend the routine use of cryobiopsy in central bronchogenic lesions.

clinical_guidelines.title: Reserve cryobiopsy for difficult cases after nondiagnostic first bronchoscopy
clinical_guidelines.condition: Central bronchogenic lesions with prior nondiagnostic bronchoscopy
specific_recommendations: If available, reserve cryobiopsy for difficult cases when the first bronchoscopy was not diagnostic.
decision_points_and_pathways: If first bronchoscopy not diagnostic -> consider cryobiopsy if available.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: This technique, if available, could be reserved for the most difﬁcult cases in which a ﬁrst bronchoscopy has not been diagnostic.

clinical_guidelines.title: Optimal number of endobronchial forceps biopsies
clinical_guidelines.condition: Central airway lesions undergoing forceps biopsy
specific_recommendations: Perform three or four biopsies to achieve best diagnostic yield.
Obtaining more than four samples does not significantly increase sensitivity.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: the best diagnostic yield can be obtained by performing three or four biopsies

clinical_guidelines.title: Prebronchoscopy coagulation screening
clinical_guidelines.condition: Patients undergoing bronchoscopy with potential bleeding risk
specific_recommendations: Do not perform routine coagulation screening in patients with no risk factors.
Perform coagulation screening in patients with known or clinically suspected risks.
decision_points_and_pathways: No risk factors -> no routine coagulation screening.
Known or suspected risks -> perform coagulation screening.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Patients with no risk factors vs those with known or clinically suspected risks
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Prebronchoscopy routine coagulation screening is unnecessary in patients with no risk factors, but it should be performed in those with known or clinically suspected risks

clinical_guidelines.title: Platelet threshold and transfusion before bronchial biopsy
clinical_guidelines.condition: Patients undergoing bronchial biopsy with thrombocytopenia
specific_recommendations: Do not perform bronchial biopsies if platelet count is <50,000/mm3.
Administer six to ten packs of platelet transfusion before bronchoscopy for such patients.
decision_points_and_pathways: Platelet count <50,000/mm3 -> defer biopsy; transfuse 6–10 packs platelets before bronchoscopy.
clinical_guidelines.contraindications_and_exceptions: Bronchial biopsies cannot be performed if platelet count is <50,000/mm3.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Bronchial biopsies cannot be performed if platelet count is <50,000/ mm3, and these patients should receive six to ten packs of platelet transfusion before bronchoscopy.

clinical_guidelines.title: Warfarin management prior to bronchoscopy
clinical_guidelines.condition: Patients on warfarin undergoing bronchoscopy/biopsy
specific_recommendations: Stop warfarin at least 5 days before bronchoscopy.
Alternatively, give low-dose vitamin K to reduce INR to <2.5.
decision_points_and_pathways: On warfarin -> stop ≥5 days before OR administer low-dose vitamin K to reduce INR <2.5.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Patients on warfarin scheduled for bronchoscopy
alternative_approaches: Low-dose vitamin K to reduce INR <2.5
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Warfarin should be stopped at least 5 days before bronchoscopy, or low-dose vitamin K should be administered to reduce the international normalized ratio (INR) to <2.5.

clinical_guidelines.title: Clopidogrel management prior to bronchoscopy
clinical_guidelines.condition: Patients on clopidogrel undergoing bronchoscopy/biopsy
specific_recommendations: Stop clopidogrel 7 days before bronchoscopy.
decision_points_and_pathways: On clopidogrel -> stop 7 days before bronchoscopy.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Patients on clopidogrel scheduled for bronchoscopy
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: The use of clopidogrel should be stopped 7 days before bronchoscopy.

clinical_guidelines.title: Aspirin management prior to bronchoscopy
clinical_guidelines.condition: Patients on low-dose aspirin undergoing bronchoscopy/biopsy
specific_recommendations: Low-dose aspirin can be continued.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Patients on low-dose aspirin scheduled for bronchoscopy
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Low-dose aspirin can be continued.

clinical_guidelines.title: Direct oral anticoagulant (NOAC) management prior to bronchoscopy
clinical_guidelines.condition: Patients on rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban undergoing bronchoscopy/biopsy
specific_recommendations: Suspend rivaroxaban, apixaban, or edoxaban for 48–72 h; this may be sufficient.
decision_points_and_pathways: On NOACs -> suspend 48–72 h before bronchoscopy.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: For patients on new oral anticoagulants (rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban), a shorter suspension period (48–72 h) may be sufﬁcient

clinical_guidelines.title: Hypervascular tumors are not a contraindication to biopsy
clinical_guidelines.condition: Carcinoids and endobronchial renal metastases
specific_recommendations: Despite higher bleeding propensity, these tumors are not a contraindication to biopsy.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Patients with carcinoids or endobronchial renal metastases
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Some tumors, like carcinoids and endobronchial renal metastases, are hypervascularized and more prone to bleed, but this is not a contraindication to biopsy.

clinical_guidelines.title: Training requirement for managing major bleeding during bronchial biopsy
clinical_guidelines.condition: Bronchoscopists performing bronchial biopsy
specific_recommendations: Bronchoscopists should be trained to manage major bleeding when performing bronchial biopsy.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: bronchoscopists should be trained to manage major bleeding when a bronchial biopsy is performed

clinical_guidelines.title: Availability of Fogarty balloon for bleeding control
clinical_guidelines.condition: Management of bronchoscopic bleeding
specific_recommendations: Ensure a Fogarty balloon is always available in the bronchoscopy suite.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: A Fogarty balloon for the management of bleeding, should always be available in a bronchoscopic suite.

clinical_guidelines.title: Use disposable brushes to reduce contamination/cross infection
clinical_guidelines.condition: Brushing of central endobronchial lesions
specific_recommendations: Use disposable brushes to reduce contamination or cross infection.
alternative_approaches: Reusable brushes (not recommended due to contamination risk)
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: it is recommended to use disposable tools in order to reduce the risk of contamination or cross infection.

clinical_guidelines.title: Handling bronchial washing when combined with other sampling
clinical_guidelines.condition: Bronchial washing in central bronchial lesions
specific_recommendations: Collect washing fluid and hold it; examine only if other specimens are not diagnostic.
decision_points_and_pathways: If biopsy/brushing diagnostic -> do not process washing.
If not diagnostic -> process washing held in laboratory.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: collect the washing ﬂuid during bronchoscopy and to hold it in the laboratory, examining the sample only if the other specimens are not diagnostic.

clinical_guidelines.title: Routine use of washing in central bronchial lesions is questionable
clinical_guidelines.condition: Central bronchial lesions undergoing washing
specific_recommendations: Routine washing in central bronchial lesions is of questionable value.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: making the value of the routine use of washing in central bronchial lesions questionable.

clinical_guidelines.title: Specimen handling for suspected infections (brushing and washing)
clinical_guidelines.condition: Suspected infectious conditions during bronchoscopy
specific_recommendations: Agitate brush in a sterile medium.
Collect washing in a sterile specimen trap.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: brush should be agitated in a sterile medium, and washing must be collected in a sterile specimen trap.

clinical_guidelines.title: Routine mycobacterial sampling not recommended in non-endemic areas
clinical_guidelines.condition: Bronchoscopy for patients in areas not endemic for mycobacterial disease
specific_recommendations: Do not perform routine bronchoscopic sampling for mycobacterial organisms on all patients in non-endemic areas.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Patients undergoing bronchoscopy in areas not endemic to the disease
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: routine bronchoscopic samplings for mycobacterial organisms on all patients undergoing bronchoscopy are not recommended in areas not endemic to the disease.

clinical_guidelines.title: Sampling of central airway lesions
clinical_guidelines.condition: Central airway lesions; endobronchial pathology visible by bronchoscopy
specific_recommendations: Conventional biopsy techniques ... must be considered the gold standard for diagnosis when an endobronchial pathology visible by bronchoscopy is present.
Biopsy forceps provide better sensitivity compared to other sampling techniques when the pattern of the lesion suggests mucosal involvement.

TBNA should be the preferred sampling instrument when there is evidence of a submucosal or peribronchial spread ... or when the superficial layers of the mucosa may not be involved or when the lesion is very necrotic.
Adding brushing to biopsy or TBNA might improve diagnostic yield, but more prospective studies are necessary to evaluate the cost-effectiveness of its use.
Washing alone is of little value ... its routine use is not recommended.
decision_points_and_pathways: If bronchoscopic pattern suggests submucosal or peribronchial involvement, use TBNA.
If macroscopic appearance suggests very vascularized tissue, use TBNA to test bleeding risk before biopsy.
If large necrotic component and biopsy shows white samples suggesting necrotic tissue, use TBNA.
After a first negative bioptic procedure, consider TBNA at repeated bronchoscopy.
Choose biopsy forceps when mucosal involvement is suggested; choose TBNA when submucosal/peribronchial spread or very necrotic lesions are suspected.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: central airway lesions; endobronchial pathology visible by bronchoscopy
alternative_approaches: Add brushing to biopsy or TBNA to potentially improve diagnostic yield (cost-effectiveness undetermined).
Avoid washing alone as a diagnostic tool for central airway tumors.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: TBNA should be the preferred sampling instrument when there is evidence of a submucosal or peribronchial spread

clinical_guidelines.title: Fluoroscopic guidance for peripheral localized pulmonary lesions
clinical_guidelines.condition: Peripheral localized pulmonary lesions (nodules, masses or infiltrates) approached transbronchially
specific_recommendations: A rotating C-arm or a biplane fluoroscope must be available to allow the assessment of the sampling instrument position both in the anteroposterior and lateral view.
Biplane control is necessary to avoid the misplacement of the instrument in front of or behind the lesion.
decision_points_and_pathways: Use biplane fluoroscopic control to confirm instrument position in AP and lateral views to avoid misplacement.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: localized pulmonary pathology (nodules, masses or infiltrates)
clinical_guidelines.monitoring_requirements: Fluoroscopic anteroposterior and lateral views to assess instrument position.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: A rotating C-arm or a biplane fluoroscope must be available to allow the assessment of the sampling instrument position both in the anteroposterior and lateral view

clinical_guidelines.title: Routine consideration of transbronchial needles and combining instruments in peripheral lesions
clinical_guidelines.condition: Peripheral localized lung lesions approached transbronchially
specific_recommendations: Transbronchial needles, showing better sensitivity, should be routinely considered for this kind of procedure.
Adding another sampling instrument may increase the diagnostic yield.
the association of needle and forceps biopsy seems to be the most appropriate and recommendable, especially in Institution where cryobiopsy is not available.
decision_points_and_pathways: If cryobiopsy is not available, choose the association of needle and forceps biopsy.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Transbronchial needles, showing better sensitivity, should be routinely considered for this kind of procedure.

clinical_guidelines.title: Minimum number of transbronchial biopsy specimens for peripheral lesions
clinical_guidelines.condition: Peripheral localized pulmonary lesions approached with transbronchial biopsy
specific_recommendations: At least six biopsy specimens should be obtained for optimizing the results.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: at least six biopsy specimens should be obtained for optimizing the results.

clinical_guidelines.title: Instrument sequence when combining needle with forceps or brushing
clinical_guidelines.condition: Peripheral localized pulmonary lesions where multiple sampling instruments are used
specific_recommendations: If the needle is used in association with forceps or brushing, it should be used first.
decision_points_and_pathways: Use needle first to avoid increased blood aspirated by the needle after biopsy/brushing.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: peripheral localized pulmonary lesions requiring multiple instruments
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: If the needle is used in association with forceps or brushing, it should be used first

clinical_guidelines.title: Use of bronchial washing and BAL in peripheral localized lesions
clinical_guidelines.condition: Peripheral localized lung lesions (non-diffuse) under bronchoscopy
specific_recommendations: When performed together with brushing or biopsy, bronchial washing shows an increase in sensitivity by only 3%, which does not justify its routine use.
BAL shows better sensitivity in malignancy with an infiltrative pulmonary pattern ... and its use may be justified if there is a suspicion of these pathological conditions.
decision_points_and_pathways: Avoid routine bronchial washing in localized lesions; consider BAL if infiltrative malignancy (e.g., bronchoalveolar carcinoma, lymphangitic carcinomatosis) is suspected.
clinical_guidelines.contraindications_and_exceptions: Use BAL selectively when infiltrative pulmonary pattern is suspected.
alternative_approaches: Brushing or biopsy as primary tools
